newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-UOB sees long way to "international" S$.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-UOB sees long way to "international" S$.

text.p: The head of Singapore's United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB), said on Friday he did not expect a speedy relaxation of rules curbing trading of the Singapore dollar on currency markets.
UOB chairman and chief executive Wee Cho Yaw told Reuters the Singapore economy was too small to allow active speculation in its currency.
"I don't see any benefit to Singapore if the Singapore dollar is internationalised. I don't see the reason for it," Wee said in an interview.
UOB has a large treasury operation which is active in a range of regional currencies against the U.S. dollar.

But, like its competitors, it is restricted by the size of Singapore dollar loans it can make and is discouraged by Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), from speculating in the currency.
The MAS scrutinises all large trades in the local currency and regularly intervenes in the market to adjust its value.
Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu has said several times in the past year that he plans to gradually relax the rules on international trading of the Singapore dollar.
He says he wants to boost the city-state as a regional centre for financial services and also encourage the trading of shares in foreign companies on Singapore's stock market.
But he has given no time frame for relaxing the rules and has not said how the MAS plans to do it.

Wee said the Singapore dollar, which has appreciated steadily against the U.S. dollar and most other major Western currencies over the past few years, could be vulnerable to manipulation if it were traded freely on global foreign exchange markets.
"The Singapore dollar market is so small, if someone manipulated the Singapore dollar I think it would be a big problem. We are not a big economy," he said.
He said he thought it would take a long time for the Singapore government to make any changes.
Asked how long it would take, Wee said: "I don't know. It is up to the government. But to me it is of no benefit at all."
Wee said UOB's treasury activities had suffered recently from volatility in forex markets.

"Over the past year I think our forex business was not very good ... I think 1995 was the best. I think 1996 will be worse. There was more volatility in the (forex) market. People were reading it wrongly," he said, but declined to give details.
